title: Can NASA predict natural disasters?
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant examine whether NASA can predict natural disasters. They explain NASA's shift toward monitoring Earth with remote sensing satellites and aircraft, and cover several programs: the 2010 GRIP (Genesis and Rapid Intensification Processes) study of how tropical storms form; GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment), twin satellites that map Earth's gravitational field and track polar ice and groundwater-related mass changes; the GPM (Global Precipitation Measurement) mission with JAXA for tracking rainfall and floods and predicting landslides; and LIDAR-based topography mapping (the LIST program, slated for 2016) to detect land deformation before volcanic eruptions and monitor fault lines. They note clouds limit laser and satellite observations. The episode then turns to near-Earth objects: asteroid impact risk, the roughly thousand kilometer-plus objects NASA tracks, nuclear deflection ideas, and the All Sky Fireball Network of internet-connected night-sky cameras. The episode closes with a listener mail letter from Amber and Ben praising the show's unscripted conversational style.
topics: GRIP genesis and rapid intensification processes

segments.title: Opening banter and NASA's shift toward Earth monitoring
segments.summary: Hosts banter and introduce the question of whether NASA can predict natural disasters, noting NASA is turning its remote sensing equipment toward Earth as private space exploration grows.

segments.title: Remote sensing and early detection
segments.summary: They define remote sensing as detecting reflected energy from afar and explain that the goal is early detection, since hurricanes, volcanoes and earthquakes cannot be stopped but warnings can save lives.

segments.title: GRIP study of tropical storm formation
segments.summary: A summer 2010 NASA project called GRIP flew a Gulf Stream jet to measure the beginnings of tropical storms; the hosts describe the proposed formation mechanism from its data, which is not yet fully proven.

segments.title: GRACE twin satellites and Earth's gravity
segments.summary: The GRACE twin satellites measure changes in Earth's gravitational field, which reflect changing mass such as melting polar ice and Greenland ice loss, with implications for sea level, climate and GPS accuracy.

segments.title: GPM precipitation tracking, floods and landslides
segments.summary: NASA and JAXA's Global Precipitation Measurement mission tracks worldwide rainfall to predict floods and landslides, recalling the hosts' visit to a landslide-hit village in Guatemala.

segments.title: LIDAR topography for volcanoes and earthquakes
segments.summary: A LIDAR-based topography program is described as improving resolution from thirty meters to five meters, letting scientists detect ground swelling before volcanic eruptions and monitor fault lines; cloud cover limits these observations.

segments.title: Near-Earth objects and asteroid deflection
segments.summary: The hosts discuss NASA's tracking of near-Earth objects, the rarity of large impacts, and proposed methods such as nuclear devices to nudge asteroids off course given enough lead time.

segments.title: All Sky Fireball Network
segments.summary: NASA's All Sky Fireball Network of internet-connected night-sky cameras, mostly on the Eastern Seaboard, tracks fireballs, and the public can apply to host a camera.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A short message break is taken during the episode.

segments.title: Listener mail from Amber and Ben
segments.summary: A listener couple who binge-listen on road trips write that they initially found the show condescending, then changed their minds after learning the conversations are not scripted.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, invite social media contact, and point to the website for more on NASA and other topics.
